The within-batch coefficient of variation (CV) was 3.46%, and the coefficient of variation among three batch means was 1.63%. At 10,000 ng/mL, Naja naja venom produced a lower ECL response than Deinagkistrodon acutus venom, Bungarus multicinctus venom, serum, and phosphate-buffered saline controls. These findings support the analytical feasibility of the competitive paper-based ECL platform and provide a basis for further matrix, cross-reactivity, stability, and clinical-sample validation.

title: Effects of Low-Intensity Exercise on Exhaled Breath Condensate Biomarkers in Healthy Horses.
abstract: Exhaled breath condensate (EBC) has emerged as a promising diagnostic tool for equine respiratory disease. However, the influence of exercise on the biomarkers of EBC remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the influence of low-intensity exercise on EBC biomarkers (hydrogen peroxide, pH, and nitrite) in healthy horses and to assess the feasibility of postexercise sample collection under real-world conditions. Twenty clinically healthy horses (ten Quarter Horses and ten Brazilian Sport Horses) were evaluated. Respiratory rate (RR) and heart rate (HR) were recorded at rest, followed by EBC collection using a collector developed by our research group. Horses then performed 10 min of trotting, low-intensity protocol, after which RR, HR, and EBC samples were reassessed. Upper airway endoscopy and tracheal lavage with differential cytology confirmed respiratory health. Biomarker concentrations were analyzed by using appropriate parametric tests. Light exercise significantly increased RR, HR, and EBC sample volumes (p < 0.05). Sample volume evidenced a weak association with ambient temperature (p = 0.014, r = 0.186) and relative humidity (p = 0.010, r = 0.218). Exercise did not significantly affect pH (p = 0.380), hydrogen peroxide (p = 0.152), or nitrite (p = 0.218). Nitrite was negatively associated with ambient temperature (p = 0.023, r = -0.056) and relative humidity (p < 0.001, r = -0.428) and evidenced a moderate positive association with hydrogen peroxide in postexercise (p = 0.004, r = 0.611). Under the conditions evaluated, light exercise did not alter equine EBC biomarker concentrations, supporting the feasibility of postexercise sampling.

title: Absolute Quantification of Tissue Composition by Raman Spectroscopy.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Raman spectroscopy captures the molecular fingerprints of living tissues without labels or tissue destruction. Translating these spectra into absolute measures of tissue biochemical composition remains a challenge owing to tissue-dependent optical properties, variations in sampling volume, and lack of normalization standards requisite for quantitative scaling. Here we introduce a scheme to derive the biochemical constituents of a tissue expressed as a percentage of the tissue wet weight, like biochemical assays, from Raman spectra measured optically. Nonlinear polynomial models of Raman spectra are trained on chemically defined phantoms that mimic the variability of the essential biochemical constituents of a tissue, accommodating spectral overlap and tissue-dependent optical effects. We validated this scheme using cartilage, a tissue fundamental to diarthrodial joint function. Cartilage is comprised of glycosaminoglycans, collagens and water that act synergistically to impart the rheological and tribological material properties essential to tissue function. Using biochemically perturbed live cartilage explants, phantom-calibrated Raman spectroscopy (PC-Raman) resolved constituent-specific changes and achieved quantitative agreement with independent biochemical assays (R2 = 0.88-0.92; slopes ≈ 1.0; 95% confidence intervals ±2.7-3.2%pt). We demonstrate that PC-Raman is applicable across the hierarchy of tissue interrogation from microscopic imaging of tissue extracellular matrix composition to macroscopic longitudinal monitoring of drug effects in-vitro using live tissue constructs and in-vivo assessments of cartilage regeneration in an equine cartilage repair model. Converting Raman spectra measurements of the essential biochemical constituents of a tissue in absolute terms (tissue wet-weight-%) allows for the non-destructive, longitudinal quantification of tissue composition in disease (tissue degeneration) and in response to treatment (tissue repair).
